items.title: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer.
items.summary: Journal: Functional & integrative genomics. Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterised by extensive genomic heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Although recurrent coding mutations in key driver genes have been well researched, large-scale sequencing studies have identified a broad array of non-coding variants which may contribute to tumorigenesis by interfering with gene regulatory mechanisms. However, understanding the functional significance of these variants remains a major challenge due to their abundance and the complexity of non-coding regulatory structures. This review outlines current computational and experimental techniques to identify, prioritise, and functionally validate non-coding variants in PDAC. We discuss in silico methods including genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapping, colocalisation, machine learning-driven functional annotation, and the use of established computational tools, in addition to epigenomic profiling technologies including, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT&RUN which define regulatory landscapes. We also emphasise new AI-based methods involving radiogenomics, AI imaging analysis and data integration, which provides novel potential to link genomic variation with phenotypic and imaging characteristics. Additionally, we highlight experimental validation techniques including reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), chromatin conformation capture methods, and CRISPR-based perturbation systems used to study variant functionality. Together, these complementary approaches establish a framework for correlating non-coding variation to regulatory mechanisms in PDAC.
items.headline: Computational and experimental methods to validate non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer
items.brief: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) involves many non-coding variants affecting gene regulation. This review outlines computational techniques like GWAS fine-mapping, colocalization, and machine learning-driven annotation, alongside epigenomic profiling methods such as ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq, to identify and functionally validate these variants.
items.why: It addresses functional interpretation of non-coding regulatory variants in cancer, a key challenge in computational genomics and epigenomics with broad relevance.
items.korean: 췌장암에서 비암호화 변이의 기능적 중요성을 컴퓨터 및 실험 방법으로 검증한다.

items.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica.
items.summary: Journal: Science advances. Abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.
items.headline: Explainable AI reveals recombination and chromatin features as key predictors of maize and Brassica subgenome evolution
items.brief: Using machine learning and explainable AI on genomic and epigenomic features, this study identifies recombination rate, chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin marks (e.g., H3K9ac, H3K27ac) as major factors predicting biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring in polyploid maize and Brassica rapa subgenomes.
items.why: It elucidates molecular and chromatin determinants of 3D genome evolution and subgenome differentiation, advancing understanding of regulatory element evolution and genome architecture.

items.title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA
items.summary: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.
items.headline: BEND 2.0 benchmark evaluates DNA foundation models for predicting effects of DNA changes and guiding design
items.brief: BEND 2.0 is a benchmark suite testing DNA language models on eight tasks from five experimental datasets, assessing their ability to predict effects of DNA variants and guide sequence design. It finds that linear readouts on frozen model representations can match or exceed native outputs, and that functional post-training improves capabilities. However, strong average effect prediction may mask weaker context-specific predictions.
items.why: It provides a rigorous, multi-task benchmark for genomic foundation models, critical for evaluating and improving models that predict regulatory element function and variant effects.
items.korean: DNA 변이 예측과 설계에 DNA 기초 모델 능력을 평가하는 BEND 2.0 벤치마크를 제시한다.

items.brief: This article explores how engaging with art affects brain function and structure, discussing neuroscience findings on perception, emotion, and cognition related to art appreciation and creation.

items.title: Predicting IGD treatment outcomes across interventions using a whole-brain functional connectome biomarker.
items.summary: Journal: Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. Abstract: BACKGROUND: Although treatment approaches have been explored in internet gaming disorder (IGD), however, little is known about the specific neural activity that is associated with treatment outcomes. This study aims to establish a treatment-sensitive network that reliably predicts treatment outcomes across different interventions for IGD. METHODS: Resting-state fMRI data were collected from 90 individuals with IGD who received one of three different intervention protocols (mindfulness meditation, approach bias modification, or retrieval-aversive conditioning training). Connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) was used to build a treatment-sensitive network to predict individual symptom reduction, then validated them on the external dataset. RESULTS: The negative (r = 0.401, p <.001) and combined network (r = 0.480, p <.001) can significantly predict a reduction of addiction severity (baseline minus post-test). Specifically, the negative network was primarily centred on the motor, subcortical, and salience networks. The positive network primarily involved cerebellar-related connections. Incorporating these into a combined model significantly improved predictive accuracy, suggesting that cerebellar-related connectivity may contribute to the prediction of intervention-related clinical improvement. Finally, the treatment-sensitive network was validated in a separate data. CONCLUSIONS: This study established a treatment-sensitive network based on the whole-brain connectome. These findings provide valuable empirical evidence for identifying biomarkers for IGD treatment and advance personalised therapeutic strategies. CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: The trial protocol was pre-registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (www.chictr.org.cn; ChiCTR2300077831(MM), ChiCTR2300075869(ApBm), ChiCTR2500095444(R-AC), ChiCTR2400090834(SAE)).
items.headline: Predicting treatment outcomes in internet gaming disorder using connectome-based predictive modeling
items.brief: Using resting-state fMRI and connectome-based predictive modeling, this study identifies brain network signatures that predict symptom reduction across different interventions for internet gaming disorder, highlighting motor, subcortical, and salience networks.
items.why: It applies multi-omics-like integrative neuroimaging and machine learning methods to predict neuropsychiatric treatment outcomes, relevant to computational genomics and neuroscience.
